summary: Nikhil Abraham, co-founder and CEO of CloudChef, describes how his company converts general-purpose bimanual robots into professional chefs working in real commercial kitchens. CloudChef's mission is to make high-quality, nutritious food affordable by automating commercial kitchen labor with culinary intelligent robots—robots that can act, sense, and reason like a chef. Rather than using expensive, unreliable humanoids, CloudChef deploys wheeled robots with two hands on a mobile base, costing approximately $12/hour with no overtime or turnover. The robot can work up to 168 hours per week, limited only by facility operating hours, with overnight prep tasks planned for the future. The core challenge is software: making the robot chef-like. The robot's culinary school involves three layers. First, it learns motion primitives through fine-tuned robot foundation models with teleoperation fallback. Second, it develops culinary understanding using thermal and visual embeddings specific to cooking, enabling it to judge food states like onion browning or shrimp doneness across seasonal and daily ingredient variation, with recipes modeled as state machines. Third, it adapts to novel kitchens, learning recipes from a single expert demonstration. CloudChef collected proprietary data by installing sensors in active commercial kitchens, gathering hundreds of thousands of live-cooked meal recordings. Their small perception model outperforms both expert chefs earning over $150,000 annually and frontier models like Gemini 2.5 and o3 at cooking progress estimation, partly because frontier models lack thermal modality. The system is 95% autonomous and 5% teleoperated, with motor skills at 80-95% of human speed. Notably, robots can optimize recipes beyond human capability—observing a chef's 20-minute process and reducing it to 14 minutes—so even operating slightly slower than human speed is economically viable. Cross-contamination is handled with washable silicone pads changed daily. CloudChef targets line cooking, which accounts for about 50% of kitchen labor costs, with dishwashing deferred. Recipe speed optimization across all cuisines remains experimental, working best where thermodynamic modeling is straightforward. Currently deployed at restaurants including Wingstar, India's Top 20 (Palo Alto), and a high-end Indian restaurant in Menlo Park, the robot alerts facility staff for ingredient resupply, with future plans for robot-to-robot communication.

sections.title: Introduction and CloudChef Mission
sections.summary: Nikhil Abraham introduces CloudChef and its mission to make high-quality nutritious food affordable by automating commercial kitchen labor with culinary intelligent robots that can act, sense, and reason like a chef.

sections.title: Form Factor: Wheeled Robots vs Humanoids
sections.summary: Compares expensive, unreliable humanoids to cheaper wheeled robots with two hands on a mobile base. These robots cost about $12/hour, always show up, and plug into any novel kitchen, learning recipes from one demonstration with robustness to ingredient, appliance, and portion variation.

sections.title: Culinary School for Robots: Motion, Food Understanding, and Adaptation
sections.summary: Describes the three-part training: motion primitives via fine-tuned foundation models with teleoperation fallback, culinary understanding via thermal and visual embeddings for food state reasoning, and recipe modeling as state machines. Covers adaptation to unseen kitchens from a single demonstration.

sections.title: Performance Evaluation and Data Collection
sections.summary: CloudChef's perception model outperforms expert chefs ($150k+/year) and frontier models (Gemini 2.5, o3) at cooking progress estimation. Thermal modality lacks internet-scale data, so they installed sensors in commercial kitchens, collecting hundreds of thousands of live-cooked meals across cuisines and seasons.

sections.title: Motor Skills, Autonomy, and Real-World Demos
sections.summary: Motor skill evals show sautéing nearly as fast as humans. System is 95% autonomous, 5% teleoperated. Shows robot cooking a two Michelin-star chef's recipe, monitoring onion browning, and reasoning about ingredient locations without pre-programming.

sections.title: Real-World Deployment and Customer Footage
sections.summary: Robot deployed in real commercial kitchens cooking for actual customers. Shows CCTV footage of robot cooking chicken wings. Robot acts as its own weighing scale via joint torque data. CloudChef is hiring for software, ML, and robotics roles.

sections.title: Q&A: Success Metrics, Taste, Form Factor, Appliances, Speed
sections.summary: Addresses success metrics, taste validation via blind taste tests, form factor (two hands on mobile base with cameras), weighing via joint torque, handling unseen appliances via knob recognition, and speed at 80-95% of human with RL expected to improve it.

sections.title: Q&A: Deployment Locations, Labor Economics, Operating Hours, Bottlenecks, Recipe Optimization
sections.summary: Robot-cooked food available at Wingstar, India's Top 20 (Palo Alto), and a high-end Indian restaurant in Menlo Park. Line cooking represents ~50% of kitchen labor cost—CloudChef's initial target. Robots can optimize recipes beyond human speed (20-min process reduced to 14 min). Robot works up to 168 hours/week, limited by facility hours. Cross-contamination handled with washable silicone pads; dishwashing deferred. Recipe speed modification is experimental, working best for cuisines with straightforward thermodynamic modeling. Ingredient resupply currently alerts facility staff; future robot-to-robot communication planned.
